title: Fronting, topic and focus

objectives.can: Notice a constituent placed before the verb or detached at the head of a clause, and consider what it marks.

explanation.summary: Hebrew sentences can put a word or phrase first that would usually come after the verb, or set a noun apart at the head of a clause and pick it up later with a pronoun. Grammarians agree that this is meaningful and disagree about how best to describe it. This lesson teaches you to notice the pattern and to weigh what it might be doing, without treating any one account as a rule.

sections.heading: Noticing the order
body: In a Hebrew story the verb usually comes first: a wayyiqtol opens its clause, and the subject follows it. In speech, in laws and in poetry the order is freer. When a clause begins with a word that is not the verb, such as an object, a phrase of time or place, or a subject, that word is said to be fronted. A fronted subject often comes with וְ: וְהֶבֶל הֵבִיא, 'and Abel, he brought'.
A fronted word is not an error and not a stylistic accident. It is a choice the writer could have avoided. The reader's job is first to notice it, and then to ask what the choice does in this place.

sections.heading: What may be fronted
body: The object may come before the verb, as in Malachi 1:3, וְאֶת עֵשָׂו שָׂנֵאתִי, 'and Esau I hated'. A phrase of time may begin a clause, as it does in Genesis 7:11, where a long phrase about the date comes before the verb. A subject may come first, and so may an independent pronoun, אָנֹכִי, אַתָּה and the rest, before a finite verb that already shows the person. The pronoun is not needed to identify the subject, because the verb's ending does that; its presence is a choice.
The reasons for a choice differ from verse to verse. That is why the discussion below speaks of what fronting may mark and does not say what it means.

sections.heading: Detached nouns: casus pendens
body: A noun, often with a relative clause, may be set at the head of the sentence and then picked up again inside the clause by a pronoun, a suffix or a repeated noun. The Latin name for this is casus pendens, 'hanging case'; some modern works say 'left dislocation' or 'dislocated topic'. In Genesis 3:12, the man says הָאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר נָתַתָּה עִמָּדִי, 'the woman whom you gave to be with me', and then the pronoun הִוא resumes it: 'she gave me of the tree'.

The detached noun names what the sentence is about. The following clause says something about it. English might write 'As for the woman you gave me, …' The resumptive element can be a pronoun, a suffix on the verb or a noun with the article, as in the repeated 'that soul' of Exodus 12:15.

sections.heading: What fronting may mark: three accounts
body: Older grammars, such as Gesenius' and Davidson's, speak of emphasis: the first word is stressed. This is an old and useful rule of thumb, and it fits many verses, but critics say it is too vague, since it does not say what kind of emphasis or what the word is stressed against.

Many recent studies use the terms topic and focus. The topic is what the sentence is about, a thing already known to the hearer or being introduced as the subject of the next stretch. The focus is the part that is new or contrasted; it answers a question or picks one possibility out of others. On this view a fronted word may be a topic (the sentence is about it, perhaps it is a shift of subject), or a focus (it is selected or contrasted). Some fronted phrases do neither; they set the scene, as dates do.

A third line of work looks at how a clause links to its neighbours: a fronted subject with וְ often marks a change of subject, a contrast with the clause before, or a background clause set beside the main line. In Genesis 42:8, 'Joseph knew his brothers and they did not know him', the second clause begins with the subject, and it sets the brothers against Joseph.

None of the three accounts explains every verse, and they can overlap. A careful reader notes what comes first, looks at the clause before and after, and says what contrast or shift of subject the context gives. If the context shows nothing, the honest answer is that the order may be only a variation.

head: Pattern
Example
May mark
rows: contrast with the clause before; selection
a change of subject; contrast; background
contrast or selection of the speaker: 'I (for my part)'
setting the scene; often no emphasis at all
names the topic and then comments on it

sections.heading: Repetition
body: Repeating a word is another way of drawing attention. David's lament for Absalom repeats 'my son' again and again, and the repetition carries the feeling. A repeated word is not a fronted one, but it belongs here, because it too is a choice of the speaker that the reader can notice and describe.

misunderstandings: A word before the verb is not always emphatic. A date at the head of a verse sets the scene, and it is not stressed.
Casus pendens is not a mistake of grammar, and it is not a sign of a corrupt text. It is a normal way for Hebrew to name a topic.

The independent pronoun with a finite verb is not redundant. Because the verb already shows the person, the pronoun does something else, which the context shows, but the nature of that something is argued.
None of these accounts is 'the rule'. They are descriptions offered by grammarians, and a given verse may fit one of them better than another.

deeper.heading: What is the basic order?
body: Whether you can say that a word is 'fronted' depends on a view of what the normal order is. Many grammars take verb–subject–object as basic, and then every word before the verb is fronted. Some argue that subject–verb–object is basic in certain kinds of clauses, such as the clauses of speech or background description, and that only in narrative is the verb-first order basic. The answer affects how much weight a fronted word is given. The lesson follows the first view for convenience and notes that the second is held by some scholars.

quoted.title: Malachi
quoted.english: But Esau I hated, and made his mountains a desolation, and gave his heritage to the jackals of the wilderness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The object, עֵשָׂו, stands before the verb שָׂנֵאתִי, with its marker אֵת. The verse before has a plain verb-first clause, וָאֹהַב אֶת יַעֲקֹב, 'and I loved Jacob'. The change of order sets Esau against Jacob. On a focus account, Esau is the contrasted item; an older grammar would speak of emphasis. Both fit.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וְהֶבֶל, a subject with וְ, comes before the verb. The verse before is about Cain's offering; this clause turns to Abel. The pronoun הוּא repeats the subject after גַּם, 'also'. A topic account sees a change of subject; a contrast account sees Abel set beside Cain. Notice that the order also fits the two brothers' parallel acts.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the man said: 'The woman whom Thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A detached noun, הָאִשָּׁה, with a relative clause, is set at the head. The pronoun הִוא resumes it, and then the verb comes: 'the woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree'. This is casus pendens. The man's speech uses the construction to name, first, the person to whom he turns attention.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And, behold, the LORD stood beside him, and said: 'I am the LORD, the God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac. The land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Another casus pendens. הָאָרֶץ with its relative clause stands first and is picked up by the suffix on אֶתְּנֶנָּה, 'I will give it'. The phrase לְךָ, 'to you', is also placed before the verb. On a focus account the recipient is stressed against anyone else who might have received it; the land is the topic of the sentence.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: The LORD will fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Both halves begin with a subject. יְהוָה יִלָּחֵם לָכֶם and וְאַתֶּם תַּחֲרִישׁוּן are set side by side, so that the one who fights is contrasted with those who keep still. The subject-first order and the independent pronoun וְאַתֶּם both lend themselves to a contrast reading; they are not required by the grammar.

practice.prompt: What does the order וְהֵם לֹא הִכִּרֻהוּ (words 4 to 6) do after וַיַּכֵּר יוֹסֵף?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew him not.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It has no function; the verse could be written in any order
It is a question
It is a command
It sets the brothers against Joseph: a new subject with וְ, in contrast with the clause before
practice.explain: The first clause is a wayyiqtol with Joseph as subject. The second begins with a new subject, the brothers, and the contrast (he knew them, they did not know him) is the point of the verse. A subject change and a contrast are the usual accounts of this order.

practice.prompt: What is שְׁכֶם בְּנִי (words 4 and 5) in relation to the clause that follows?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Hamor spoke with them, saying 'The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter. I pray you give her unto him to wife.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A vocative address to the brothers
A detached noun naming the topic, resumed by the suffix on נַפְשׁוֹ, 'his soul'
A second subject of a different verb
The object of the verb חָשְׁקָה
practice.explain: Hamor sets Shechem at the head, 'Shechem my son', and then says 'his soul longs for your daughter'. The suffix -וֹ on נַפְשׁוֹ picks up the detached noun. This is a casus pendens.

practice.prompt: What do אַתָּה (word 4) and וְאָנֹכִי (word 10) set up in David's speech?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: Then said David to the Philistine: 'Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast taunted.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A mistake in the text
A command to the Philistine
A repetition with no sense
A pair in contrast: 'you come with a sword … but I come in the name of the LORD'
practice.explain: Each clause begins with an independent pronoun and a participle. The parallel order, with the pronouns first, sets the two men side by side, and the means they bring are put against each other.

practice.prompt: What is the function of אָנֹכִי (word 13) and בַּדֶּרֶךְ (word 14) before the verb נָחַנִי?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who hath not forsaken His mercy and His truth toward my master; as for me, the LORD hath led me in the way to the house of my master's brethren.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: They are the same word repeated
אָנֹכִי names the speaker as topic, 'as for me', and the phrase of the way is put before the verb as well; the speaker is stressing what the LORD did for him
They are a question
They are the verb's subject and object
practice.explain: The servant first praises the LORD, then turns to himself. Two things come before the verb, the pronoun and the phrase of place; the suffix on the verb is the object 'me'. The pronoun is not needed to show the person, which the suffix already shows; the order suggests that the servant is speaking of his own case.

practice.prompt: What stands before the verb נִבְקְעוּ (word 14) in this verse?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Phrases of time, which set the scene; they need not be emphatic
A detached noun with a resumptive pronoun
The object, which is stressed above all
A question word
practice.explain: The verse opens with date after date, and the verb comes after them. This is fronting, but its purpose is to place the event in time. It shows that not every word before the verb is a focus.

check.prompt: How does the word order of וְאֶת עֵשָׂו שָׂנֵאתִי differ from that of the clause before it, וָאֹהַב אֶת יַעֲקֹב?

quoted.title: Malachi
quoted.english: But Esau I hated, and made his mountains a desolation, and gave his heritage to the jackals of the wilderness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It has no object
There is no difference
It has the object first, where the earlier clause has the verb first; the change sets the two brothers against each other
It is a question where the other is a statement
check.explain: The earlier clause is verb-first (a wayyiqtol). The object אֶת עֵשָׂו is placed before the verb here. It is read as contrast with Jacob. The written order is the only difference.

check.prompt: What might the fronted subject וְהֶבֶל (word 0) mark?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A change of subject from Cain to Abel, perhaps with a note of parallel or contrast
A question
Nothing at all, because subjects must come first
A command
check.explain: The preceding verse is about Cain. A subject with וְ before the verb turns to the other brother. The reading 'topic shift' or 'contrast' is reasonable; the grammar does not force one of them.

check.prompt: What does הִוא (word 6) do after the detached noun?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the man said: 'The woman whom Thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a verb
It is an object of the verb
It resumes the detached noun הָאִשָּׁה as the subject of the verb that follows
It is a second detached noun
check.explain: After a long relative clause the sentence needs its subject again. The pronoun הִוא takes it up. This is the usual form of casus pendens.

check.prompt: What does the suffix on אֶתְּנֶנָּה (word 18) refer to?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And, behold, the LORD stood beside him, and said: 'I am the LORD, the God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac. The land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Jacob
The LORD
The detached noun הָאָרֶץ, 'the land', set at the head of the sentence
No one in particular
check.explain: The suffix 'it' picks up הָאָרֶץ, so the land is the detached topic. The phrase לְךָ before the verb is also fronted, which suggests that the one who receives it is stressed.

check.prompt: Which statement about the order of יְהוָה יִלָּחֵם לָכֶם וְאַתֶּם תַּחֲרִישׁוּן is within what grammarians say?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: The LORD will fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Only the first clause is fronted
Subject-first order and the pronoun וְאַתֶּם can set the two parties against each other, though the grammar does not require the contrast
The order proves that the verbs are in the past
The order is a certain sign of a command
check.explain: Both clauses begin with the subject. A contrast between the LORD and the people fits that order, and many take it so. It is a reading, not a rule.

check.prompt: What is the relation of כָּל־אֹכֵל חָמֵץ (words 11 to 13) to הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא (words 15 and 16)?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; howbeit the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses; for whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: They are two separate subjects
The first is the subject and the second the object of the same verb
The second is a vocative
The first is a detached noun phrase, 'whoever eats leaven', and the second resumes it as the subject of 'shall be cut off'
check.explain: The phrase with כָּל names the person, then הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא picks it up. The structure is a casus pendens, a common one in laws. The word כִּי before it gives the reason for the earlier command.

check.prompt: What does the independent pronoun אָנֹכִי (word 0) add to אֶעֶרְבֶנּוּ?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him; if I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame for ever.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The person, which the verb does not show
The tense, which the verb does not show
A note of contrast or selection, 'I (for my part)', since the verb already shows the person
A negative sense
check.explain: The ending of אֶעֶרְבֶנּוּ already shows the first person. The pronoun is not needed to identify the speaker, so its presence is read as stress. Here Judah offers himself where others had not.

check.prompt: What does the final clause וְאָנֹכִי וּבֵיתִי נַעֲבֹד אֶת יְהוָה (words 29 to 33) set against the choices before it?

quoted.title: Joshua
quoted.english: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a question
It is a command to the others
It sets the speaker and his house against the others: 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD', with the subject placed first
It repeats them
check.explain: The earlier clauses name the possible objects of service, 'whom', 'the gods of the fathers', 'the gods of the Amorites', and put the choices before the hearers. The last one begins with the subject and his household and then gives the verb and its object. The change of order marks the contrast.

check.prompt: What can one say about the order הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי (words 9 and 10) in the woman's answer?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the LORD God said unto the woman: 'What is this thou hast done?' And the woman said: 'The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The order means the woman is not answering
The subject is placed before the verb: it can be read as the focus of the answer to 'what is this you have done?', or as a topic, and the order alone does not decide
The serpent is first because it must be
It is certainly an emphasis on the serpent, and nothing else can be said
check.explain: A subject before the verb is not the usual order in narrative, and an answer that names the serpent first suits a focus account. But a reader should say that the context supports the reading, not that the order proves it.

check.prompt: What does the repetition of בְּנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנִי בְנִי (words 10 to 13) do?

quoted.title: 2 Samuel
quoted.english: And the king was much moved, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept; and as he went, thus he said: 'O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It marks a change of subject
It marks a command
It carries feeling: the king repeats the name and the word 'my son' in grief
It is a scribal error
check.explain: The words come again and again in the lament. Repetition in speech like this is read as a sign of feeling; no grammatical change accompanies it.

reading.why: The questioning in the garden contains a detached noun resumed by a pronoun (verse 12) and answers that begin with the subject (verses 12 and 13). Reading these verses you can compare the verb-first narrative frame with the speakers' own word order.
